Taxpayer funds spent on pro-Trump ads despite pledges of private super PAC backing.
Evidence: AdImpact data, White House PSA defense, Common Cause lawsuit
#Aletheia #USPol #Accountability

The administration claimed taxpayer-funded promotional ads were educational public service announcements and that private super PACs would cover campaign-adjacent media.
Stated Judgement: (+0.5, 0.0) — Good Preference

Audits reveal nearly $22 million in taxpayer funds bankrolled the ads, with $10 million spent after the president promised private funding, violating anti-propaganda laws.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.85, -0.80) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception.
Taxpayer funds were diverted into unauthorized partisan advertising while public oversight mechanisms were bypassed.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 16.5, z: 4)

- Taxpayer Ad Funding: FAIL (-0.90, -0.85) — Public funds used for political ads.
- DOJ Search of Rep. Omar: COND (-0.60, -0.50) — Politically contested probe.
The U.S. government continued funding pro-Trump promotional spots despite a federal judge's stop order and presidential pledges of private super PAC financing.

The Poison:
Misusing public coffers for unapproved political propaganda breaks legal firewalls between state machinery and campaign apparatuses.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing WHO pays (taxpayers vs private donors) and WHAT the ads are (partisan campaigning vs neutral PSAs) to skirt federal spending laws.

Social Physics Analysis:
The administration runs a Smart Selfish Maneuver, utilizing public tax dollars for partisan messaging while projecting a veneer of educational necessity, shielding political motives behind bureaucratic pretexts.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil. F_neg dominates as state resources are extracted for partisan gain.

The Unavoidable Truth: Taxpayer funds were improperly spent on partisan advertisements in violation of federal restrictions.

The Unavoidable Lie: These promotional spots qualified as objective public service announcements.

It hurts to watch public resources meant for community welfare get siphoned off into political theater while citizens carry the cost.

Brothekanon:
Saying a super PAC is paying and then billing taxpayers for ten million bucks after a court says stop is a wild way to run things.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Government spent millions on Trump ads. And, federal agents raid Ilhan Omar's home

The government is using millions of taxpayers' dollars on pro-Trump ads, even after the president said this would not happen. And, federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar's D.C. home.

Actual Article Body:
By

Brittney Melton

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

The U.S. government continues to pay for ads promoting President Trump, even after he announced that his MAGA Inc. super PAC would take over funding. A federal judge ordered the ads to be taken down, yet they remained on air. An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer funds have been spent since the campaign began in late September. Almost $10 million of that was spent after Trump pledged on an Oct. 5 Truth Social post to fund the campaign privately. The White House has called the ads public service announcements, but a lawsuit by Common Cause and others argued they were funded without congressional approval, violating restrictions on taxpayer-funded publicity and propaganda.

President Trump leaves the stage after speaking during an election rally in Syracuse, New York on Oct. 9, 2026.
                
                    
                    Alex Wong/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

Trump has ramped up his campaign travel ahead of the midterm elections. He rallied supporters in Youngstown, Ohio, last night and is heading to Alaska today. More events are planned for later this week. He has been trying to encourage his supporters to vote by telling them to pretend he is on the ballot.

Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in Washington, D.C., yesterday morning. Omar, D-Minn., says the search was politically motivated by the Trump administration. The Department of Justice told NPR in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant," approved by the DOJ, as part of an ongoing federal investigation. Current and former federal officials with knowledge of the search who were not authorized to speak publicly confirmed the details, revealing that this multi-year probe includes whistleblower complaints and focuses on allegations of immigration fraud.

The safest way to protect yourself from measles when traveling is to be vaccinated.

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles resurgence in decades. More than 3,600 confirmed cases and two deaths have been reported as of late September. Outbreaks in several states and exposures in public places like bars, sports stadiums and public transit have raised concerns about travel safety. Almost all U.S. measles cases involve unvaccinated individuals, and as the outbreaks grow in some states, the risk of exposure is getting higher. When Lee Krasner was asked in a 1978 interview what she was doing while her husband Jackson Pollock was becoming so famous, she said, "I was working all the time." Krasner is shown above, at work, in 1981.
                
                    
                    Ernst Haas/Getty Images

The Metropolitan Museum of Art's new blockbuster exhibition showcases the works of two 20th-century artists. Jackson Pollock is well-known for his drip paintings. His wife, Lee Krasner, has often been overshadowed by her husband. This show finally gives Krasner the recognition she deserves. With more than 120 pieces on display — 74 from Krasner and 48 from Pollock — the show highlights Krasner as a titan of Abstract Expressionism, too. Check out some of the photos from the exhibit.
